intro: In 1740, a girl on a Pennsylvania farm and a boy on a South Carolina rice plantation woke up under the same king. One would grow up free. One would not. A century later, a family floated everything they owned down the Ohio River toward Illinois, past a slave state on one bank and a free state on the other. This unit is the story of how those two worlds became one country, and how the argument between them grew as the country grew.

You will see how land shaped the thirteen colonies, who worked and who was free, and how colonists got used to running their own towns. You will follow the fight with Britain from a tax on paper to a war, and watch fifty-five sweating men in a shut-up room build a new kind of government. Then you will ride the steamboats and rails west, watch Illinois become a state, and learn what that growth cost the people who were already here.

Along the way you will read the actual words of the Declaration, the Constitution and the law that made Illinois free. You will look at numbers from ship records and the census. And you will keep asking the unit's big question: the founders promised liberty for all. Who got it, when, and what did it take?
bigQuestion: The founders promised liberty and equality. Who got it, who was left out, and how did the promise get stretched?

timeline.t: English settlers build Jamestown, Virginia, the first lasting English colony
Virginia's House of Burgesses meets; the first enslaved Africans arrive in Virginia
William Penn founds Pennsylvania and promises freedom of worship
The Stamp Act; colonists protest taxes without a vote
The Declaration of Independence is approved on July 4
The British surrender at Yorktown with French help
The Constitution is written in Philadelphia; the Northwest Ordinance bans slavery north of the Ohio
The Bill of Rights is added
The Louisiana Purchase doubles the country; Lewis and Clark set out the next year
The Erie Canal opens; steamboats and canals speed up trade
The Trail of Tears: the Cherokee are forced west

test.q: Why did New England colonists turn to fishing and shipbuilding?
choices: Rocky soil made farming hard, and the sea and forests were rich
Fish were the only food they liked
test.why: Geography shaped work: poor farmland but rich fishing grounds and tall timber.

test.q: Which region grew tobacco and rice on plantations using enslaved labor?
test.why: Hot, wet lowlands in the South suited cash crops that needed huge amounts of labor.

test.q: How was slavery different from indentured servitude?
choices: Slavery lasted for life and passed to children; an indenture ended
test.why: Both worked without pay, but only the servant's contract had an end.

choices: The forced voyage of enslaved Africans across the Atlantic
The trip of Puritans to Massachusetts
test.why: It was the middle leg of the Atlantic trade, carrying captured people in chains.

test.q: What did colonial assemblies control that gave them real power?
test.why: Because assemblies decided how money was spent, royal governors needed their cooperation.

test.q: What does no taxation without representation mean?
choices: People should not be taxed by a body they have no vote in
Taxes should be paid in tea
test.why: Colonists objected to being taxed by Parliament, where they had no representatives.

test.q: What did the Intolerable Acts do?
choices: Closed Boston Harbor and punished Massachusetts
test.why: The punishment for the Tea Party pushed the other colonies to unite with Massachusetts.

test.q: According to the Declaration of Independence, where does government get its power?
choices: From the consent of the governed
test.why: This was the Declaration's biggest idea and a break from the old idea of kings.

test.q: Why was the winter at Valley Forge so deadly?
test.why: No battle was fought, but about two thousand soldiers died of sickness and cold.

test.q: What was the main weakness of the Articles of Confederation?
choices: Congress could not tax or enforce laws
test.why: Without taxes or an army, the national government could not pay debts or keep order.

test.q: What is an example of checks and balances?
choices: The president can veto a law from Congress
test.why: The veto lets one branch limit another, and Congress can override it in turn.

test.q: What did the Northwest Ordinance say about the land north of the Ohio River?
choices: It would stay a colony forever
It would become equal states, with no slavery
test.why: The 1787 law set the path to statehood and banned slavery in the territory.

test.q: What did the Louisiana Purchase of 1803 do?
choices: Doubled the size of the United States
test.why: The United States bought the land from the Mississippi to the Rockies from France.

test.q: What happened on the Trail of Tears?
choices: The Cherokee were forced west and thousands died
Lewis and Clark reached the Pacific
test.why: In 1838, about sixteen thousand Cherokee were marched to Oklahoma; roughly four thousand died.

test.q: How did the cotton gin affect slavery?
choices: It made cotton profitable, so slavery grew
test.why: Fast cleaning meant more cotton fields and more enslaved people to work them.

write.prompt: The Declaration says all men are created equal. Make a claim: in the years from 1740 to 1840, did the United States keep that promise, break it, or do both? Use at least three pieces of evidence from this unit.
tips: Claim: one clear sentence. Kept, broken or both, and for whom.
Evidence: pick from the Middle Passage, who could vote, the three-fifths clause, the Northwest Ordinance, the Bill of Rights, the Trail of Tears.
Reasoning: after each piece of evidence, explain how it supports your claim.
The other side: name one fact someone who disagrees would use, and answer it.
Use dates and real people. Say roughly or about when you use a rounded number.
